theory.intro: A shape has **line symmetry** when folding it along some line makes the two halves match exactly; that line is an **axis of symmetry**. It has **rotational symmetry** when a turn of less than a full circle about its centre leaves it looking the same.
facts: Every shape has order at least $1$, so **order $1$ means no rotational symmetry**.
A **regular** $n$-sided polygon has $n$ axes of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $n$.
For **irregular** shapes the two can differ: a parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus has $0$ axes of symmetry but rotational symmetry of order $2$.
The axis of symmetry is a line, not part of the shape itself — a parabola with a vertical axis and its vertex on the $y$-axis has axis $x=0$.

workedExamples.solution_text:
a. Reflecting in the $y$-axis leaves the parabola unchanged. A half-turn about the origin makes it open downward. **Line symmetry only.**

b. Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the line's slope. A half-turn about the origin maps the line onto itself. **Rotational symmetry only.**

c. Reflecting in the $y$-axis or turning about the origin leaves the circle unchanged. **Both.** The circle is unchanged by every rotation about its centre, not just a half-turn.

 d. Reflecting in the $y$-axis produces a decreasing curve. A half-turn about the origin moves the curve below the $x$-axis. Neither transformation leaves it unchanged. **Neither.**

foundation.solution_text:
Each axis of symmetry runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
There are $3$ such lines, so the triangle has $3$ axes of symmetry.

Two axes pass through the midpoints of opposite sides and two pass through opposite corners.
That gives $4$ axes of symmetry.

Only the two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides fold the rectangle onto itself.
A fold along a diagonal does not match the halves, so there are $2$ axes of symmetry.

The single axis runs from the apex down to the midpoint of the base.
The two equal sides swap onto each other, so there is $1$ axis of symmetry.

No fold line makes the halves match — folding along a diagonal or a midline leaves the slant pointing the wrong way.
The parallelogram has $0$ axes of symmetry.

Turning the regular pentagon about its centre, it matches its start after each $72^{\circ}$ turn.
In one full turn that happens $5$ times, so the order of rotational symmetry is $5$.

A regular hexagon matches itself after each $60^{\circ}$ turn.
That happens $6$ times in a full turn, so the order of rotational symmetry is $6$.

A rectangle matches itself after a $180^{\circ}$ turn, and again after a full $360^{\circ}$ turn.
So the order of rotational symmetry is $2$.

A scalene triangle has all sides different, so it only returns to its original position after a full $360^{\circ}$ turn.
So the order of rotational symmetry is $1$ (no rotational symmetry).

development.solution_text:
Reflecting the line in the $y$-axis tips it the other way, so there is no line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin maps the line onto itself, so it has rotational symmetry of order $2$.
Rotational symmetry only.

Reflecting in the $y$-axis leaves the circle unchanged, so it has line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin also leaves it unchanged, so it has rotational symmetry.
It has both.

Reflecting in the $y$-axis gives a different curve, so there is no line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin also gives a different curve, so there is no rotational symmetry.
Neither symmetry.

Reflecting in the $y$-axis gives a different curve, so there is no line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin maps the curve onto itself, so it has rotational symmetry of order $2$.
Rotational symmetry only.

Reflecting in the $y$-axis leaves the horizontal line unchanged, so it has line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin moves it to the other side of the $x$-axis, so it has no rotational symmetry.
Line symmetry only.

The triangle folds onto itself along the vertical line through its apex and the midpoint of its base.
No other fold makes the halves match, so it has $1$ axis of symmetry.

A regular octagon has an axis through each pair of opposite sides and each pair of opposite corners: $8$ axes.
It matches itself after each $45^{\circ}$ turn, so the order of rotational symmetry is $8$.
$8$ lines of symmetry and order $8$.

The two diagonals are the only fold lines, giving $2$ axes of symmetry.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn maps the rhombus onto itself, so the order of rotational symmetry is $2$.
$2$ lines of symmetry and order $2$.

mastery.solution_text:
No fold line makes the halves match, so there are $0$ axes of symmetry.
But a $180^{\circ}$ turn about the centre maps the shape onto itself, so the order of rotational symmetry is $2$.
$0$ lines of symmetry and order $2$.

Reflecting the two branches in the $y$-axis swaps them for a different pair, so there is no line symmetry about the $y$-axis.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn about the origin maps each branch onto the other, so it has rotational symmetry of order $2$.
Rotational symmetry only.

The three blades are made of straight segments and all point around the centre in the same direction, so no fold line makes the halves match: $0$ axes of symmetry.
The shape matches itself after each $120^{\circ}$ turn, so the order of rotational symmetry is $3$.
$0$ lines of symmetry and order $3$.
